Mr. Speaker, I doubt whether I shall ever be as volatile as the hon. member for

The Budget-Mr. John MacLean Hull but I hope the house will find my comments just as interesting as his. At the outset I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on the capable, competent and courteous manner in which he presented the budget to the house. In the course of this debate-it has been a short debate so far-the minister has been criticized in rather a destructive way. Of course, in such a responsible office as his he should expect criticism; for he cannot hope to please everyone all the time. But I do believe some of this criticism is unjustified.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) made comments at length upon the budget and I should like to deal with some of the points which he attempted to make in this house. He saw fit to suggest that the government had increased taxes at this time only so that in two years time they might decrease taxes. I suggest, Mr, Speaker, that this sort of statement is not in keeping with the hon. member's position in the house. Who likes to raise taxes? To think for one moment that we are going out of our way to raise taxes so that in two years time we can decrease taxes is absolutely fantastic. Do hon. members think that I am pleased, or any member of this government, or any member in this house, for that matter, is pleased when taxes are raised? I know that I myself, and I am sure this feeling beats eternally in the hearts of everyone across Canada when budget time comes, hope that taxes wifi be decreased. However, that is not always possible. I point out this to the hon. friends to my right. If taxes are decreased next year and the following year, or three years from now, it will only be because of the policies followed by the Minister of Finance and by this government.
There has been much talk this afternoon, and there was much talk in the latter part of Thursday evening, with regard to our decrease of taxes late in 1957. It is even being intimated that perhaps this was a pre-election scheme of some sort of the Conservative party-

speechtext: Was it not?

speechtext:
see my friends are following me very closely. I think it is fairly well recognized-and it is recognized by some of the best financial people across this country-that our decrease in taxes at that time, along with our higher expenditures, the two of them combined, were probably the most important forces in stemming and halting the business decline in 1958.
Then, we have this statement by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that the


Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is breaking faith with the electorate; he is not fulfilling his promises. He even moved an amendment to this effect. He said the Prime Minister stated that there was no great difficulty to be encountered in bringing about deductions in taxes and also having increases in pensions. The Prime Minister probably did make this statement, but what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River forgot to mention in this house was that there was a budgetary surplus of $282 million in 1956; that there was a forecast budgetary surplus of $305 million in 1957 which-and I want to be fair about this-the former minister of finance took upon himself to apply in only his own inimitable fashion and in devious ways to cut down the surplus to $152 million. We have then the Prime Minister making those statements before the election of June, 1957, statements based on huge surpluses two years running by the former Liberal government.
Is it too far out of line to say that the Canadian people took this for granted, that when we were in office, if there was a surplus, we would take that surplus and use it for the benefit of the Canadian people? Surely it is misconstruing the facts entirely and underestimating the intelligence of the Canadian people to say that they believed this hodgepodge; that what was said at that time dealt with economic conditions during the recession or when financing needed to be done in such a huge manner as was needed last year and is needed to be done this year.
The hon. member talked about unemployment, but he is not the only one who talked about it. The hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) talked about unemployment. I would like to talk about unemployment. This is something I want to point out to the Liberal party. Last year and this year they have taken a keen interest in the problem of unemployment. Where their interest was in 1954 and 1955 I have failed to discover. I have searched Hansard for those years and have failed to find one comment by any member of the Liberal front benches about the importance of the disastrous unemployment in 1954 and 1955. Certainly, all unemployment is bad. Let us not forget that. Regardless of what explanation or excuse we place upon it, nobody wants unemployment. I do not want unemployment. We would all like to see everybody with employment.
During the debates on this topic we are forever talking about statistics and figures. The government brings out statistics; the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) brings out his statistics; and we have a battle royal. But those statistics and figures do not mean

anything to the man on the street who is out of work. This is a problem that was thrown upon us when we assumed office, a problem that was not of our doing, and do not think for one moment that the people across this country recognize that it is any different. And yet, we have our winter works program where we pumped millions of dollars into the program. We have a statement by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) on November 11, 1958 with regard to what he thought of the winter works program. He said in Toronto, Ontario, according to a Canadian Press report of November 11, 1958:
The federal government's winter work program has been made too late to be of maximum effect this winter.
The government's attack on jobs has been "unco-ordinated, unplanned-actions which have resulted in large expenditures without corresponding results in terms of employment."
During the summer there was a seasonal improvement in trade and employment. Canadians showed vigour and initiative in combatting recession and preventing it from sliding into depression, he added. This was in large part due to the social and economic policies brought into operation since 1935 by Liberal governments, policies which had kept up consumer purchasing and cushioned the impact of recession.
He says in effect that if unemployment gets worse it will be the government's fault; their policy and program have no value. Then he goes on to say there was an improvement during the summer in employment and, of course, this was due to the social and economic policies brought into operation since 1935 by the Liberal government. What he says in effect is that if things get worse it is the fault of the present Conservative party; if things get better it is only because the Liberal government was in power for 22 years. What a remarkable statement for the Leader of the Opposition to make. Possibly he has never made a more inaccurate and misleading statement since he assumed office.
On unemployment the opposition currently talks in generalities. I am, of course, concerned with the general picture, but I am more vitally concerned with the situation as it exists in the city of Winnipeg. During the debates on unemployment and during this debate here we have heard their cries about the terrible picture of unemployment and how terrible it is today. Let me point out to them that the situation in the city of Winnipeg at the present time is better than it was in 1955. Where were the cries of the member for Kenora-Kainy River (Mr. Benidickson) in 1955 about unemployment or, for that matter, the cries of any of those on the Liberal front benches? They are not fooling the people of the city of Winnipeg on this very important matter.

There is that chatter again. We hear that chatter every so often. Having regard to the way the subamendment is worded and its ambiguity, it is impossible for me to even think of supporting it. We have heard repeated pleas with regard to reducing capital expenditure. The latest plea to that effect was made by the hon. member for Hull. This would be fine in itself. I am one of those who support such a proposal. We must reduce government expenditures in every way possible.
As a matter of fact, the government has reduced expenditures in this budget when you consider our total expenditures in the light of the increased services and the increased population. However, at this point in our economy when we are emerging from a recession I cannot see for the life of me, and I have looked over the budget quite thoroughly, how we can cut expenditures any further.
There are three main branches of expenditure. One of them has to do with national defence. Expenditure on national defence in any free country is very large. It does not appear at this time that much can be done with regard to cutting expenditure on this department. As Mr. A. G. Gardiner sets out in his "Life of Harcourt":
What a good thing for the world it would be if all nations were altogether insolvent. How much less mischief they would do.
But as he noted, "Even beggars will fight." This has been true ever since Victorian days. Beggars have learned to fight with modern weapons and to pay for a good stock of the most up-to-date killing machines, even if they can pay for little else. Perhaps this example is a little far-fetched but in reference to the world scene today a disarmament policy has not been put into effect and at the present time we cannot afford to cut our expenditures on national defence.
Then we come to social security which is another item of major government expenditure. I hope that no one here is suggesting that we cut old age pensions or family allowances. Certainly I for one believe that all Canadians realize that social security has to

be paid for by way of taxes, and I do not think there is anyone who would not expect an increase in the rate of taxation in order to balance the old age security fund. I do not think there is anyone who believes this is unfair at the present time. Let us be realistic.
I should like to say a few words about our old age pensioners. Many of our old age pensioners are barely existing on the $55 a month they receive, and I think most members will agree with me when I say that old age pensions should be increased and perhaps the age qualification should be reduced to 65 years. I am in favour of these two things as are many members of this house. The only obstacle that remains is how to accomplish them.
The government has received Dr. Clark's report which is the result of an extensive investigation into the present social security system in the United States in relation to Canada's old age pension scheme. I have read the report thoroughly, and I must say that Dr. Clark made a very complete and thorough investigation. This report is now in the hands of the government and the existing problems in connection with old age security must be met in the near future. How far such provisions should go and what form they should take are still open problems. There are two things that appear to be needed: one is stability in real terms for payments, and the second is an agreement on a stable proportion of the national income to be devoted to this purpose.
A simple system is needed, in my estimation, to tie the payments to the movements of national money income. I believe the old age pensioner across Canada realizes that this government has his interests at heart, and since this is the case we should stand prepared to alleviate any of the sufferings of our senior citizens. I have every confidence that this assistance will be forthcoming by way of legislation after a thorough study has been made of the fine report submitted by Dr. Clark.
However, I do not believe that this will be enough. I would think that after the government has studied this report in all its details, a national conference should be called to consist of the government and all interested agencies across this country as well as representatives from the various provinces. Then, this conference could re-evaluate the present situation of the old age pensioner. Something must be done and the problem must not be left to the haphazard guessing game of other days. The policy must be a long range one and must be for the benefit of old age pensioners across the country in the years to come.

The Budget-Mr. John MacLean
There is another item, probably the last major item of government expenditure mentioned by the hon. member for Hull, and that is the servicing of the national debt. Surely, no one could suggest that this be discontinued. After these three items, defence, social security and the servicing of the national debt, have been dealt with, there are really very few places for the government to economize. At this time, therefore, we are faced with the only alternative and that is to raise some taxes, yet not raise them too high so as to prohibit the expansion of our economy. Certainly, some budgetary deficit would be appropriate in order to ensure the continued economic recovery of this nation.
Our economy has become dependent on growth and, therefore, very substantial increases in both domestic and foreign demand will be necessary in order to keep pace with the growth of the Canadian labour force and its increased efficiency. We have two problems, therefore, to solve in our present day Canadian economy. One of these problems is unemployment and the other is inflation. It is important, and I believe all financial experts agree with me on this, that the soundness of the Canadian dollar be preserved.
In this connection it was mandatory that an attack be made on last year's deficit, as it was made by the Minister of Finance. I do not believe there is anyone who disagrees with the statement that inflation creates more unemployment than it cures. Not only does it do this, but it affects the savings and investments of a great many people and, in the end, it would lower productivity. It is important, therefore, that we attack inflation. Why do we not go all the way and raise taxes still further in an attempt to balance the budget? This would not be a proper thing to do for, as the minister has pointed out in his budget speech, we have to combat inflation and yet ease unemployment. We have to have an expanding economy, that is our industrial output must be increased. We have to be careful just how high we raise taxes to ensure that our economy does not retract but keeps on expanding. It is not possible at this stage in our economy to ensure an expanding economy other than by way of a deficit budget, although this deficit is a great deal smaller than the deficit of last year.
Our national budget is supposed to provide us with a picture of our finances which will enable us to reorganize the economic life of our country. Our national budget should give us an indication of whether or not the government is really grappling with the problems prevailing in our economic society. I believe in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, that the budget brought down by our Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Rdbichaud Finance does fulfil these conditions. Since it does this, I believe it reflects the outstanding characteristics of the present government. Let us never forget that the manner in which we govern our country is linked with the manner in which we govern our finances. The wealth of this nation is not measured by statistics relating to fiscal policy; it can be measured only by the amount of goods and services provided to our people and by the standard of living they enjoy as well as their freedoms as evidenced during their daily life in this great country.
It is the dream of every minister of finance to build a perfect budget. Perhaps before too long the present minister may have occasion to do just that. I hope I am sitting in this house when he does. This year's budget has been described in various ways in speeches by hon. members and in the various newspapers across the land. It has been described as a belt-tightening budget, as a recovery budget and in the Winnipeg Free Press in my own home town as a castor oil budget. Some of these things, in essence, are true. I should like to name this budget and call it a sincere budget. I would call it a sincere budget because it is typical of the responsible attitude of this government toward the people of Canada.
In closing I should like to reiterate the statement the Minister of Finance made while presenting his budget last year. This represents the true position of this government. "We stake our unwavering belief in Canada's destiny, and we shall strive to meet the challenge of our responsibilities."

It is my intention, in the course of my remarks this evening, to elaborate to some extent on this lack of consistency in the present policy of the government, as compared with the pre-election stand of its members, and particularly with the stand taken by those who have been sitting on the opposition side of this house in the years past.
My criticism of the present budget will be based on six different points, all the factors concerning which I intend to elaborate, which show the complete lack of consistency, even the lack of policy of the present government. This lack of policy on the part of the government was clearly indicated in an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail on Saturday, April 11, under the title "No Policy To Guide Him". This newspaper which is commonly known as being generally not too unfriendly to the present administration clearly states that present tax increases will also increase costs and prices in every sector of Canada's economy. An over-all national program to include consideration of projects which would be of lasting and definite benefit to Canada, should be the aim of the government under existing conditions.
In my own constituency of Gloucester, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) has been offered the possibility of providing employment, and I mean permanent and repeated seasonal employment, to a large number of fishermen and shore workers in different fishing communities. I have placed before the minister requests for a wharf extension at Maisonnette; for the replacement of a wharf at Lower Caraquet which was partly disintegrated in a storm last fall; for the construction of a wharf at Pigeon Hill, to accommodate the fleet of 60-odd fishing boats of the area; for improvements to the entrance of Tracadie Harbour, and Ferguson Gully. Those are the kind of public works projects which should receive priority in the preparation of public works estimates. A new post office building or a new federal building will provide employment during the construction stage, but it will not add to the economy of
[Mr. Robichaud.l

an area as much as a public wharf which can accommodate a fishing fleet and bring in new industries to the communities concerned. In delaying the construction of a public wharf, where its construction has been proven economically justified, the department is contributing to the extension of the serious unemployment situation such as exists today in my constituency, and in other fishing areas of the maritimes.
A request is before the department for the construction of a new wharf at Bathurst. There is a progressive town with a paper mill, lumber mills and other industries, but nevertheless it is deprived of proper shipping facilities. The matter has been before the department for some time and it is urgent that a decision should be reached without delay to provide Bathurst harbour with adequate docking facilities to permit shipping by water the production of its industries.
An important factor in Canada's economy is the disposal of our surplus primary products. Time will not permit me to elaborate on this fifth factor, which shows the lack of direction of the present government and its inconsistency in the application of its trade policy. This is the government which had pledged itself to switch some of Canada's trading eggs out of the United States basket. This is the government which has boasted of its accomplishments in increasing trade and beginning the shift away from an overwhelming percentage of Canadian purchases in the United States. This is the government which, on the eve of the last general election, claimed to have a real plan worked out in detail in order to give opportunities to provide markets. Nevertheless, this is the same government under whose administration the value of merchandise exports in 1958 amounted to $4,890 million, compared with $4,909 million in 1957, a decrease of $19 million, and this notwithstanding the gifts of wheat shipments made under the Colombo plan and without at the same time taking into consideration the annual increase in our population. This is the same government which has lead the country to unwarranted restrictions of quotas on the part of the United States, on imports of certain Canadian products such as oil and base metals.
I am not surprised, that on April 1, 1958, the day following the last general election, a mining company in my constituency, the Brunswick Mining and Smelting, made the announcement of its decision to cease operation at once and place its equipment and machinery in mothballs until the advent of better days to come.
A sixth factor which is clearly noticeable from the present budget is the failure of the

government to reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined reallocation of taxing powers so that provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities. Here again, time will not permit me to discuss this subject at length this evening. May I be permitted, however, to remind the house of the words of the present Minister of Finance, then the private hon. member for Eglinton who, when speaking on the 1954 budget debate as reported at page 4212 of Hansard of April 28, 1954, said:
There is the hard fact of the situation, and there is the fact that makes this sophistry we have listened to from the Minister of Finance and others so completely unrealistic. You can talk today about concurrent rights on the part of the provinces, the Minister of Finance and others can say that the provinces have just as much right as they ever had to levy income tax on persons or corporations hut, Mr. Speaker, you must take account of the fact that the federal government is already taxing to the limit in those fields.
Further along he continued:
Nothing will change it except action on the part of the dominion and the provinces to come together to reach an agreement in this field and then action on the part of parliament and the legislatures in consequence.
It is not surprising that a government with no policy to guide it would devote so little attention to a subject of such cardinal importance. It is a surprise, however, that the Minister of Finance has forgotten so soon his own statements as well as those made by the Prime Minister during the last federal election campaign.
I know that I have only a few minute left at my disposal. I have elaborated on six different points which demonstrate the com' plete failure on the part of the government to cope with existing problems and I have illustrated its inconsistency and lack of policy in the administration of the affairs of the country. I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will be quite familiar with the six points I have mentioned this evening. So far as the other members on the government side are concerned, I would refer them to pages 3992 and 3993 of Hansard for April 12, 1954, where they will find those six points included in the amendment of the official critic of the opposition on the 1954 budget presented by Mr. Abbott.
In view of the contents of the present budget, I cannot see how the hon. member and those on the government side who were sitting in the opposition at that time cannot vote in favour of the amendment introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson).
We were accused then of failing to reduce taxes when in reality the budget offered $36
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud million in tax reductions as compared with increases of $352 million in the present budget. We were accused of failing to reduce unnecessary expenditures when our total expenditures in the 1954 budget were estimated at $4,460 million, as compared with total expenditures of $5,660 million, or an increase of $1,220 million; yes, an increase of $1J billion in the present budget. We were accused of failing to improve the efficiency of the administration when in fewer than two years of administration the present government has increased the civil service force by over 9,000 and has failed to show evidence of waste and extravagance in any of the departments.
We were accused of ignoring the problem of unemployment when we had a temporary
570,000	registrations for jobs at the national employment service which, two months later, had practically been entirely absorbed owing to the policies of the then government, against a present force of over 800,000, which has constantly remained at a level 30 to 40 per cent higher since the present government took office.
We were accused of failing to retain and regain markets for our surplus primary products when the expanding trade and the real plan to provide markets promised in the 1958 election campaign have failed to materialize.
We were accused of failing to reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined re-allocation of taxing power, so that municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities, when the present budget offers no relief whatsoever in this field and when the present government refuses to meet with the provinces and municipalities to discuss their mutual problems.
With the exception of the war years the Liberals produced an almost continuous series of surpluses which were associated with years of progress and prosperity. In a spectacular fashion, under a Conservative government, the pattern has been altered and the lower taxes promised in 1957, and partially applied in 1958, have been of short duration. In fact, the over-all picture is that Canadians were offered a thin slice of $200 million in tax reductions out of a promised $500 million reduction, and fewer than 10 months later they were being asked to pay back this same $200 million, plus an additional amount of $152 million, making a total additional burden of $352 million in a full year. This, is quite different from what most Canadians were led to expect when they listened to election promises and decided to let new political hands take over the administration

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early in this session, when I came back to the House of Commons, I found my seat had been changed. You may recall that last session I was sitting beside you, to your right, facing the opposition. If by-elections between the two sessions did not modify the Progressive Conservative representation of March 31, 1958, they had, at least, the effect of establishing me in this part of the house. However, be assured that I am happy about it, because the effect was to take me further away from the opposition, and anyone getting away from the present opposition can truly have the feeling of getting nearer to the Canadian people. That is why tonight I want to speak on the problems of education, of international trade and also on another subject, if time allows.
Mr. Speaker, since I came to this house, I was astonished to note with what care, and 
also sometimes with what indifference, a good number of hon. members avoid referring to the significant problem of education. When dealing with such matters we must always go back to the confederation pact of 1867, because our parliamentary thoughts and actions must be ruled by our constitution. We may say immediately that if the Canadian constitution is a good one, it should be respected. If it is bad, it should be amended with the consent of all parties concerned. But as long as it is not changed, we should respect all that it prescribes.
As far as I am concerned, I would be in favour of amending the federal pact with regard to some matters of a physical nature, like the trans-Canada highway and hospital insurance. We know that since 1867-it is not difficult to confirm it-Canadian economy has developed considerably. Economic problems have changed and we have now eleven governments, i.e. ten provincial governments and one federal government. When these governments want to carry out their projects, they sometimes, in certain fields, feel with regard to the constitution as if they were stifled by a straight jacket.
In regard to problems of a practical nature, it would therefore be desirable to amend the Canadian constitution. At a federal-provincial conference, it would be proper to set up a national economic council, with economists from the federal government and from each province as members, who would study and report their views to the various governments, precisely in order to co-ordinate the production of each and to allow an appropriate development of our natural wealth.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is a field which, in my humble opinion, cannot be touched and that is the field of education. In 1867, the two main races and the four provinces of the time created the federal government of which we are now part. In doing so, they wished to set up in this country a federal system, that is the Canadian federal system.
But what is federalism? It is a system of association between autonomous governments; in other words, the governments adhering to and composing such a system, are not subordinated to one another, but are co-ordinated governments. Under such a system, those governments co-operate in common tasks, such as, for instance, under article 95, in immigration and agriculture. Those same

governments respect the exclusive rights of each. Under such a system, those same governments know that they cannot do indirectly what they are prohibited to do directly by the constitution.
Those principles of Canadian federalism were recognized and sanctioned several times by decisions of the privy council in London, especially in the Great West Saddlery case, 1921, in the Edwards case, in 1930, and in the aeronautics case, in 1932.
Mr. Speaker, if the province of Quebec, in 1867, adhered to the confederative pact, it was precisely to safeguard its rights, prerogatives, traditions, as well as its teaching and educational system.
Under the Canadian constitution, article 91 provides that the federal government may legislate for the peace, order and good government, in all matters not coming under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. Under section 93 of the constitution, the provinces are granted exclusive rights in the field of education.
But what is meant by an exclusive right? It is a right that belongs peculiarly to the holder and cannot be shared, except with mutual consent. An exclusive right is of a higher order than an ordinary right, and even overrides a priority right, a relative right. In its own field, it is an absolute right.
But it is not enough to have rights; there must be the financial means to exercise them. So the fathers of confederation had the foresight to include subsection 2 of section 92, which grants to provinces the financial means of exercising their prerogatives. I am referring to direct taxation, within the provinces, for the purpose of raising income to meet provincial needs.
That is the basis of the position taken by some provinces, and particularly the province of Quebec, in claiming exclusive rights in the educational field. It is a matter of justice, of right and of freedom.
Mr. Speaker, whatever formulas may be invented, whatever contortions of the mind are resorted to, I think sooner or later, we shall have to come back to the spirit of the confederation pact of 1867, and hand back to the provinces that want them the taxation fields they need to discharge their exclusive prerogatives and rights.
In 1901, the following statement was made by Boucher de la Bruyere, superintendent of education in the province of Quebec:
The majority of the people in the province of Quebec insist on controlling their own schools, and in no way favour the encroachment of the federal government in the educational field outside the limits set by Canada's constitution.
The Budget-Mr. Allard
A few years ago, Mr. John P. Rowat, then chairman of the Protestant committee on education in the province of Quebec, in discussing federal government interventions into the field of education, made the following statement:
I oppose such interventions, because they go against our laws and against the traditions of the majority in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, the only case where, under subsections 3 and 4 of section 93 of the confederation pact, the federal government may subsidize schools is where the schools of a minority group in a province are being deprived of their rights.
But under what principle do many Canadians and those of the province of Quebec in particular object to the active role of the federal government in the field of education? It is because of the principle of the responsible government which we have been enjoying in this country since 1841. Responsible government requires ministers to account to the people for their management and expenditures. Now for an administrator to be able to account for his managership, he must control the moneys he is distributing. And it is precisely this control which defeats the purpose of the confederation pact and which the province of Quebec is not prepared to accept.
An objection might be raised to the effect that the federal government can give unconditional grants. But such a procedure is fraught with danger, and the best evidence I can marshal on that score was given by the former justice minister in the Liberal government, Mr. Garson, who in March 1952 said in this house in the course of a debate:
If they were large enough to be worthwhile, the dominion treasury simply could not defend handing out these large sums of money to the provincial governments without assuming some responsibility as to the manner in which they would be spent.
It will be recalled that when the Liberals were in power they did indirectly what the constitution forbade them to do directly in this field. During the winter of 1957, they passed two pieces of legislation under which they established an arts council and granted financial assistance to universities. To justify their encroachment upon this field of education they referred to an excerpt from the judgment of Lord Atkin, of the privy council in London, in a case concerning unemployment insurance. That part of the judgment reads as follows:
That the dominion may impose taxation for the purpose of creating a fund for special purposes and may apply that fund for making contributions

The Budget-Mr. Allard In the public interest to individuals, corporations or public authorities could not as a general proposition be denied.
But while they were referring to that judgment, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals were hiding the truth and knowingly failed to communicate the other part of the same judgment of Lord Atkin, of the privy council, which rightly limits the governmental activity in the field at issue. That second part of the judgment reads as follows:
But assuming that the dominion has collected by means of taxation a fund, it by no means follows that any legislation which disposes of it is necessarily within dominion competence.
It may still be legislation affecting the classes of subjects enumerated in section 92 and, if so, would be ultra vires. In other words, dominion legislation, even though it deals with dominion property, may yet be so framed as to invade civil rights within the province: or encroach upon the classes of subjects which are reserved to provincial competence. It is not necessary that it should be a colourable device, or a pretence. If on the true view of the legislation it is found that in reality, in pith and substance, the legislation invades civil rights within the province or in respect of other classes of subjects otherwise encroaches upon the provincial field, the legislation will be invalid. To hold otherwise would afford the dominion an easy passage into the provincial domain.
Briefly, such are the law and the precedents that establish the exclusive competence of the provinces in the field of education. The province of Quebec is then perfectly right in claiming its exclusive rights in that field. But while it was offering resistance, claiming its dues and being thus deprived of money, the Quebec universities were thus less favoured by the provincial state than the other universities in the other provinces.
In fact, the Quebec universities received, in 1956, provincial subsidies for general purposes, equivalent to 20.83 per cent of their budget. In Ontario, that proportion was 32.43 per cent; and, in the west, 45.52 per cent.
To settle that problem, formulas were suggested, among which a reduction in taxes, the surrendering of the direct taxation field, the restitution of levied overtax and the deduction of taxation.
But in my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, the main remedy for the provinces under the constitution would be the gradual return of their taxation fields to the provinces who want them back, so that they may exercise their financial prerogatives guaranteed by the federal pact.
The federal government has to face so many problems in national and international affairs, that it is ill-advised to deal with matters in which it is not concerned.


If the Liberals, when they were in power, had looked after their business, the country would not have been so badly administered and it would not have been left to us in such a state of unemployment and inflation.
As they are now in opposition, Mr. Speaker, we often hear them hold forth and make interjections, and the questions we are asked precisely arise from that die-hard centralizing policy they have embarked upon.
In that regard, I recall a statement made by the Liberal member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) who on January 29, said in this house, as reported on page 133 of Hansard, and I quote:
Therefore, I repeat that in my opinion the fathers of confederation, in good faith, did not think in terms of universities when section 93 was enacted.
Mr. Speaker, I must reply to that statement made by the member for Megantic that I have never heard such a superficial and inadequate interpretation of the Canadian constitution.
It was rightly said: in 1867, in addition to Laval University, McGill University had already been erected on the Burnside estate by the royal institute for the advancement of science. Established in 1856 under chapter 54, Victoria 19, the higher education income and investment fund was to be distributed by the superintendent of lower Canada schools to such universities or colleges as were approved by the governor in council. This higher education income fund, as well as education, the permanent university fund and the royal institute, are mentioned in the fourth schedule to the British North America Act as part of the assets taken over by the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. How then can someone rise in this house and say that section 93 does not include education at all levels, including the university level?
Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the present government will restore things to their proper place. I know the right hon. Prime Minister shows respect for the Canadian constitution. I should like to quote from a statement he made during the last session before a delegation of the Canadian conference on education:
Education must remain under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. The sections of the British North America Act which grant to the provinces the exclusive jurisdiction in the field of education must stay intact. Such constitutional rights are not apt to be amended. All Canadians must recognize the necessity of maintaining the constitution inviolate in this respect.

In turn, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) September 6 of last year, while explaining his estimates to the house, stated:
Now I say, Mr. Speaker, on the matter of Canadian universities and about the attitude of the present government, that while the formula contained in the present agreement has not so far been such as to be viewed with favour in the province of Quebec, if there is any formula or modification of the present agreement which anyone cares to put forward which would permit the institutions of higher learning in the province of Quebec to participate, and which is in keeping with the national interest, we as a government are prepared to give it serious consideration.
That is why if the Quebec government cares to offer a suggestion, to make an official proposal, an appropriate and constructive one, I am positive that this government will consider it with great care and that, eventually, a decent solution will be found in this field.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall allow my hon. friend to ask questions when I am through with my speech. It will then be a distinct pleasure to answer his questions.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, before going any farther I should like to sincerely congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who last Thursday night presented in this house a budget which was most favourable to economic recovery. He completely confused those in the opposition who seemed to prophesy a billion dollar deficit. His statement revealed our economy is presently healthy and progressive under an intelligent administration. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, through the federal parliament we deal with national problems, we also must turn our thoughts to international issues.
I wanted to inform this house of a particular observation I made during my stay in New York as a parliamentary observer last fall, during the thirteenth regular session of the general assembly of the United Nations Organization. The house certainly remembers that the six main institutions of the United Nations are:	the general assembly, the
secretariat, the security council, the trusteeship council, the economic and social council and the international court of justice. Now, one of these bodies, i.e. the general assembly, mainly functions through a bureau and seven larger committees. Those committees are: the
The Budget-Mr. Allard committee on political and security questions, comprising control of armaments; the special policy committee, which during the thirteenth session studied the opportunity of maintaining the police force in Gaza; the committee on financial and economic questions, which considered, during the thirteenth session, technical assistance to underdeveloped countries; the committee on social, cultural and humanitarian matters; the committee on trusteeship comprising non-autonomous territories; the committee on budgetary and administrative matters and, finally, the committee on legal matters. It is therefore, in the economic and social council, one of the six bodies mentioned, and also in the third important committee, that economic problems are discussed. Some people, when speaking of the United Nations Organization, think that it has attained no concrete or practical results and they point out, amongst others, the field of politics. Indeed, if we consider some aspects like armaments, for instance, we find that since 1946 there has not been much progress yet in this respect. More than 863 meetings took place, either at the atomic energy commission, or the disarmament committee, or even at the security council. But nations have always developed new armaments. However, in the economic and social fields, commentators recognize that the United Nations have attained practical results.
One can wonder if, in the economic field, the United Nations Organization has used its influence to improve trade relations, labour conditions and production methods for or between its members.
On February 18, 1946, a resolution adopted by the economic and social council recommended the establishment of an international organization on trade and employment. An international conference was therefore held in Havana, from November 1947 to March 1948. It was intended at the time to promote the economic progress of underdeveloped countries as well as to improve their standard of living. At that conference, 53 countries, including Canada, adopted regulations known as the Havana charter. To give permanent form to the international organization on trade and employment, a provisional committee was created and Mr. L. D. Wilgress, of Canada, became the first chairman of the executive committee. But, since that event which took place in Havana and which was designed to regulate international trade and employment, there has been no practical result, except that resolution coming every year before the

The Budget-Mr. Allard economic and social council. That resolution is urging member nations to approve, through their respective domestic legislation, that principle of international organization of trade and employment.
It seems that the U.S. congress, at first reticent for several years, would support that principle. Canada, for its part, would wait until the United States and the United Kingdom take legislative action in this matter. Pending the belated setting up of such an international organization, some countries have joined together and concluded general agreements on customs tariffs and trade. These agreements are known as GATT. In 1947, at Geneva, 23 countries adhered to that multilateral trade agreement and, in 1949, at Annecy, 10 other countries took part in another series of negotiations on customs tariffs. But in spite of those international efforts to smooth international trade relations, the United Nations does not seem to sponsor any co-ordinated system in the field of production. It would be advisable if member nations agreed to determine and co-ordinate the nature of their production. For instance, here in Canada, in Ontario and Quebec, and particularly in the eastern townships, where I come from, we produce textiles; other countries like Japan, the United States and England are producing identical or similar textiles. The result is, therefore, that without wishing it perhaps, we are sustaining against each other a very keen competition, a very unhealthy one. Would it not be preferable then, that countries competing in the manufacture of a similar product should agree to diversify their production and coordinate their industrial activities? In that regard, would it not be desirable within the United Nations, through the economic and social council, or within the North Atlantic pact, to set up some sort of body, namely an economic guidance council, in order that such member countries might study the problems relating to the diversification of their production and the co-ordination of their trade and industrial activities? Indeed, such an organization might be set up within the UNO or under the North Atlantic pact. Article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty reads as follows:
The parties will contribute toward the further development of peaceful and friendly international relations by strengthening their free institutions, by bringing about a better understanding of the principles upon which these institutions are founded, and by promoting conditions of stability and well-being. They will seek to eliminate con-

flict in their international economic policies and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.
Since the North Atlantic treaty was signed on April 4, 1949, economic alliances have begun to take shape, such as Benelux, the coal and steel pool, EURATOM, the six-power customs union, the European common market plan, but all these moves are outside NATO, and the leading American partners of the alliance are kept outside.
Mr. Paul-Henri Spaak, secretary general of NATO and chairman of the North Atlantic council, stated on April 8, 1959, during a brief press conference held at the St. Hubert airbase:
However, in the economic field, very little has been done: we shall have to lay particular stress on co-operation in this field. In that regard, I think the NATO countries should co-ordinate their efforts with regard to helping underdeveloped countries.
The fifteen NATO countries will have to do much more and much better in that field and NATO should be the ideal instrument for the co-ordination of endeavours intended to contribute to the economic growth of underdeveloped countries.
So, whether through UNO, NATO or the commonwealth, Canada should continue to initiate economic endeavours. I am inclined to believe that the allies will defeat communism and will restrain its effects to the extent that they will co-ordinate their efforts and their economic relations.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it 10 o'clock?
